Series::traverse¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signatures¶

Series::TraverseAccessor Series::traverse;

SeriesTraverseProxy Series::traverse() const;
SeriesTraverseProxy Series::traverse(std::initializer_list<ExtractSpec> on_specs) const;
SeriesTraverseProxy Series::traverse(std::span<const ExtractSpec> on_specs) const;

Every finder method (find_ge, find_eq, find_all, find_first, …) is reachable both directly on the accessor and on the proxy returned by traverse(...). Each finder returns a TraverseMatch.

What It Does¶

traverse is a content search over a Series. You describe a condition on the values, and it returns the coordinates of every position that satisfies it — together with the matched values, the flat offsets, and helpers to pull the same positions out of another Series.

This is a place where Series deliberately steps outside the tensor-library mould. The usual tools answer “where?” only indirectly:

  • a comparison such as x.ge(5.0) returns a boolean Series the same shape as x — you still have to turn that mask into positions yourself

  • x.nonzero() turns a mask into a [K, rank] coordinate block — but you have to build and pass the mask, and you get back only raw coordinates

traverse folds that whole pipeline into one call and hands back a small result object you can query several ways:

auto hits = temps.traverse.find_ge(30.0);

hits.count();            // how many positions matched
hits.coords();           // [K, rank] int64 grid coordinates, row-major order
hits.values();           // [K] the matched values (differentiable)
hits.linear_indices();   // [K] flat row-major offsets
hits.split_indices();    // rank separate [K] index columns
hits.select_from(other); // gather those same positions out of `other`

Reach for traverse whenever the question is “which elements satisfy this, and where are they” rather than “reshape / reduce / transform every element.”

The Accessor And The Proxy¶

traverse on its own searches the whole Series:

auto hits = grid.traverse.find_ge(6.0);

traverse({ ...selector... }) first narrows to a sub-view and searches only that:

auto row1_hits = grid.traverse({std::int64_t{1}}).find_ge(5.0);   // row 1 only
auto last_col  = grid.traverse({pluss::Slicing::Ellipsis(),
                                std::int64_t{2}}).find_ge(6.0);    // last column

The selector list is the same view-only language accepted by traverse_slice() — scalar indices, positive-step slices, SliceAll(), NewAxis(), Ellipsis(). Coordinates in the result are relative to the traversed view, not to the original Series: after traverse({1}) on a 3 x 3, a TraverseMatch has rank() == 1 and its coordinates index the three columns of row 1.

Returns¶

Series::TraverseAccessor (the member) / SeriesTraverseProxy (from calling it) A lightweight search entrypoint bound to the owning Series. Reading traverse copies no data and computes nothing until a finder runs.

Gradient¶

The search itself — coordinates, counts, flat offsets — is pure integer bookkeeping and carries no gradient. But the two operations that produce values are differentiable:

  • match.values() is a gather from the searched Series; its backward routes sensitivity to exactly the matched positions.

  • match.select_from(other) is a gather from other; its backward routes sensitivity into other at the matched positions.

So a traverse result can sit inside a training graph as long as gradient flows through values() / select_from() and not through the coordinates.

Example¶

auto grid = pluss::make_series({
    {10.0, 4.0, 7.0},
    {2.0, 9.0, 6.0},
    {8.0, 1.0, 5.0},
});

auto hits = grid.traverse.find_ge(6.0);

std::cout << "count=" << hits.count() << "\n";
std::cout << "coords=" << hits.coords();
std::cout << "values=" << hits.values();

Output¶

count=5
coords=pluss::Series(shape=[5,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=10, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 0],
  [0, 2],
  [1, 1],
  [1, 2],
  [2, 0]]
values=pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[10, 7, 9, 6, 8]

Coordinates come back in row-major order, so values reads [grid[0,0], grid[0,2], grid[1,1], grid[1,2], grid[2,0]].

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • A finder always returns a defined TraverseMatch. “No matches” is count() == 0 with empty coords() / values(), never an undefined result or an exception.

  • With traverse({ on }), result coordinates are relative to the sub-view, and rank() is the sub-view’s rank.

  • find_all / find_if require the mask shape to match the traversed shape exactly — no broadcasting.

  • Coordinates and counts are non-differentiable; only values() and select_from() carry gradient.

  • Match order is row-major (last axis fastest), the same order nonzero() uses.

Summary¶

traverse is the value-driven search surface:

  • one call from “condition” to “coordinates + matched values + flat offsets”

  • traverse searches the whole Series; traverse({on}) searches a sub-view

  • results are a queryable TraverseMatch, not a bare mask

  • values() and select_from() are differentiable; the index data is not
